lessons.title: Lesson 1: Turning a skill into a clear offer
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-sentence offer that says what you sell, to whom, and why they should choose you.
This lesson builds toward: Given a skill people already ask you for, you will write a one-sentence offer that says what you do, who it is for and what makes you different, in words that sound like you.
A business starts with something people need and will pay for. Think about what neighbors already ask you to do: cook for parties, braid hair, fix things, watch kids, cut grass.
A clear offer says what you do, who it is for, and what makes you different. For example: "Weekend meal prep for busy working families on the east side, with home-style food at a fair price."
Ask the AI to help: "I am good at cooking Caribbean food and people ask me to cater parties. Help me write three one-sentence offers for a small catering business, each for a different kind of customer." Then pick the one that sounds most like you.
Step by step:
- List what people already ask you to do.
- Pick one skill people would pay for.
- Ask the AI for three one-sentence offers for different customers.
- Choose and edit the one that fits you best.
Words to know:
- Offer: a short statement of what you sell and who it is for.
- Customer: a person who pays for what you sell.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to write three one-sentence offers for a skill you have. Pick one and change it so it sounds like you.
You can now turn a skill into a clear, one-sentence business offer.

options: Weekend meal prep for busy families on the east side, home-style at a fair price
check.why: It says what you do, who it is for and what makes you different.

check.q: The AI gives you three offers, but none sound like you. What do you do?
options: Pick one and change the words so it sounds like you
check.why: The offer should be yours, so you edit the best one to fit you.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Pricing so you do not lose money
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Work out a price that covers your costs and pays you for your time.
This lesson builds toward: Given the costs and hours for one job, you will calculate a price that covers your costs and pays you for your time, checking the AI's math yourself with a calculator and comparing local prices.
Many small businesses charge too little. To set a fair price, add up your costs: supplies, gas or bus fare, any fees, and your time.
Ask the AI to set up the math with you, using your own numbers: "I cater a party for 20 people. Food costs $120, containers $15, gas $10, and it takes me 8 hours. I want to earn $18 an hour. What price covers it?" Then check the math yourself with a calculator.
AI does not know local prices. Look at what others near you charge, and ask a free business advisor. Taxes and licenses are real costs too: check with your city or county, your state, and the IRS (irs.gov) about what applies to you.
Step by step:
- List every cost for one job: supplies, travel, fees.
- Decide what you want to earn per hour, and count your hours.
- Ask the AI to add it up using your numbers.
- Check the math yourself with a calculator.
- Compare with local prices and ask an advisor.
Words to know:
- Cost: money you spend to do the work.
- Profit: the money left after you pay all your costs.
Official sources:
- IRS: Small business and self-employed
Try it now: Pick one job your business would do. List the costs and hours, ask an AI assistant to work out a price that covers them, then check the math yourself.
You can now set a price that covers your costs and your time, and check the math yourself.

check.q: Which cost do many small business owners forget to count?
check.why: Your time is a cost too, so the price must pay you for your hours.

check.q: The AI says your price should be $150, but your own costs add up to $160. What do you do?
options: Recheck the math with a calculator and fix the price
check.why: AI can make math mistakes, and a price below your costs loses money.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Finding free business help
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Find a free business advisor near you.
This lesson builds toward: Using the SBA's resource partners page, you will find a free business advisor near you and plan what to ask, writing down their name, contact and three questions.
You do not have to figure it all out alone. The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) works with resource partners that help people start and grow businesses.
SCORE is a network of volunteer business mentors who give advice at no cost. Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) offer counseling and training. Women's Business Centers offer free to low-cost help for women starting or growing a business. Veterans Business Outreach Centers serve veterans and military families.
These advisors can help with licenses, taxes, loans and plans for your area. Bring your questions and your one-page plan.
Step by step:
- Open the SBA's resource partners page.
- Find SCORE, an SBDC or a Women's Business Center near you.
- Write down the name and how to contact them.
- Write three questions to ask, such as which licenses you need.
Words to know:
- Mentor: an experienced person who gives you advice.
- SBA: the U.S. Small Business Administration, the federal agency that helps small businesses.
Official sources:
- SBA: Resource partners
Try it now: Find one free business advisor near you through the SBA's resource partners page. Write down their name, contact and three questions to ask.
You can now find free, official business help near you.

options: A network of volunteer business mentors who advise at no cost
check.why: SCORE is an SBA resource partner with volunteer mentors at no cost.

check.q: You are not sure which licenses your catering business needs. What do you do?
options: Ask a free business advisor and check your city, county and state
check.why: Advisors and your local and state offices know the rules for your area.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Writing your business description and a post
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a three-sentence business description and one social media post.
This lesson builds toward: Given your offer, you will write a three-sentence business description and one social media post with an AI assistant, with every promise true and only safe contact details.
A short description tells people who you are, what you do and how to reach you. You can use it on a flyer, a business card, or a free business page.
Ask the AI: "Write a warm three-sentence description for my weekend meal-prep business for busy families. Then write one short Facebook post announcing my first menu." Ask for a version in another language if your customers need it.
Edit so it sounds like you. Only promise what you can deliver. Use a business phone or email you are comfortable sharing publicly, not your home address.
Step by step:
- Ask the AI for a three-sentence description using your offer.
- Ask for one short social media post.
- Edit both so they sound like you.
- Check that every promise is true and the contact info is safe to share.
Words to know:
- Social media post: a short message with words and maybe a picture, shared on apps like Facebook or Instagram.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to write a three-sentence description of your business and one short social media post. Edit both to sound like you.
You can now write a short business description and a post that sound like you.

check.q: What three things does a short business description tell people?
options: Your prices, your bank and your age
Your competitors, your fears and your goals
Who you are, what you do and how to reach you
Your home address, your hours and your family
check.why: A description says who you are, what you do and how to reach you.

check.q: The AI's post promises "same-day delivery" but you cannot do that. What do you do?
check.why: Only promise what you can deliver.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Keeping simple money records
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set up a simple free sheet to track money in and money out.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Sheets or Excel on the web, you will create a simple money sheet and record sales and expenses, with all five columns, totals, and entries made the same day.
Keeping records helps you see if you are making money, and you will need them at tax time. You can start with a free spreadsheet like Google Sheets or Excel on the web.
Ask the AI: "Help me set up a simple sheet for my small business with columns for date, what it was, money in, money out, and notes. Show me how to add up each column." Then make it yourself.
Write down every sale and every expense the same day, and keep receipts (a photo works). Ask a free business advisor or a tax professional what records you need for taxes. Do not type bank account numbers into the AI.
Step by step:
- Open Google Sheets or Excel on the web.
- Make columns: date, what it was, money in, money out, notes.
- Ask the AI how to add up each column.
- Write down every sale and expense the same day.
- Keep a photo of each receipt.
Words to know:
- Spreadsheet: a grid of rows and columns for numbers and lists.
- Expense: money you spend for the business.
- Receipt: proof of a purchase or payment.
Try it now: Make a simple sheet in Google Sheets or Excel on the web with the five columns. Add three pretend sales and two expenses, and add up money in and money out.
You can now keep simple money records for a small business in a free spreadsheet.

options: To see if you are making money and be ready at tax time
check.why: Records show if you make money and you need them for taxes.

check.q: You bought $30 of supplies but lost the paper receipt. What could you have done?
options: Taken a photo of the receipt the same day
Typed your bank number into the AI
Guessed the amount at tax time
check.why: A photo of each receipt keeps a record even if the paper is lost.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Answering customers and putting it all together
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write polite customer replies and finish your one-page business plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a customer message or complaint, you will write a polite reply and put your work together into a one-page business plan, offering only what you can afford and including every part of the plan.
Good service brings customers back. AI can help you write polite replies fast: confirming an order, saying you are fully booked, or handling a complaint calmly.
For a complaint, ask: "Write a calm, kind reply to a customer who says the food arrived late. Apologize, explain we will fix it, and offer a small discount next time." Read it and make sure the offer is one you can afford.
Now put your work together on one page: your offer, your price and costs, your description and post, a note about your records, and the free advisor you found. That page is the start of your business plan.
Step by step:
- Ask the AI for a polite reply for a common customer message.
- Check every promise before you send it.
- Put your offer, price, description, post, records note and advisor on one page.
- Bring the page to your free advisor meeting.
Words to know:
- Business plan: a written plan for what your business sells, to whom, and how it will make money.
Try it now: Final task: make a one-page plan with your offer, a checked price that covers your costs, a three-sentence description, one social media post, and the contact of a free business advisor near you.
You can now plan, price and promote a small business and know where to get free expert help.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Offer No offer, or it does not say what, who for, or why you. One sentence with what you do, who it is for and what makes you different. Edited so it clearly sounds like the learner. Price covers costs Price below costs, or the math was not checked. Lists costs and hours, and the price covers them with the math checked by hand. Compared with local prices and noted taxes and licenses to ask about. Description and post Missing, or makes promises the business cannot keep. Three-sentence description and one post, true and with safe contact info. Includes a second-language version for customers who need it. Free advisor No advisor named. Names a SCORE, SBDC or Women's Business Center advisor with contact details. Lists three questions to ask at the meeting. One-page plan Parts are missing or spread across pages. All parts are on one page, including a note about money records. Ready to bring to an advisor meeting, with a sample customer reply. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What goes on your one-page business plan?
options: Offer, price and costs, description and post, records note and a free advisor
check.why: The one-page plan puts all your work together in one place.

check.q: You are fully booked this weekend and a customer asks for an order. What do you send?
options: A polite reply that you are booked and offering another date
check.why: A polite, honest reply keeps the customer coming back.
